batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::07 IO, Network, Data Formats::06 Regular Expressions

cards.front: Which three classes make up the java.util.regex package?
cards.extra: Pattern is the compiled regex, Matcher is the matching engine over an input string, and PatternSyntaxException reports a malformed pattern.
cards.example:
java.util.regex.Pattern p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("a+");
java.util.regex.Matcher m = p.matcher("aaa");
try { java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("["); }
catch (java.util.regex.PatternSyntaxException e) { System.out.println(e.getDescription()); }

cards.front: How do you obtain a Pattern instance?
cards.extra: The compile step builds the internal automaton once; calling it per match is wasteful, so compiled patterns are commonly cached in static final fields.
cards.example:
var p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("dog");
System.out.println(p.matcher("dog").matches()); // true - compile is the factory

cards.front: Given a Pattern p, how do you get a Matcher for a string s?
cards.extra: The matcher binds one pattern to one input and holds mutable state such as the region bounds and the last match position, so it must not be shared between threads.
cards.example:
var p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("dog");
var m = p.matcher("dog");
System.out.println(m.matches()); // true: Pattern creates Matcher; no public constructor

cards.front: What kind of exception is PatternSyntaxException?
cards.back: An unchecked exception signalling a syntax error in a regex pattern
cards.extra: Because it is unchecked it is not declared in throws clauses, so a malformed user-supplied pattern only surfaces at the compile call.
cards.example:
try {
    java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("[");
} catch (RuntimeException e) {
    System.out.println(e instanceof java.util.regex.PatternSyntaxException); // true, unchecked
}

cards.front: Why is it safe to share one compiled Pattern across threads but not one Matcher?
cards.extra: A Matcher holds per-input state such as region bounds and the last match index, so sharing one matcher across threads corrupts results, while sharing the pattern is safe.
cards.example:
java.util.regex.Pattern p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("a+"); // immutable: share across threads
java.util.regex.Matcher m = p.matcher("aaa"); // mutable state: keep it local
System.out.println(m.find() + " " + m.find()); // true false: find advances the state

cards.front: Java's java.util.regex syntax is most similar to which regex flavour?
cards.extra: Not grep, awk or POSIX; Java borrows Perl syntax but with significant additions such as possessive quantifiers and Unicode property escapes.
cards.example:
var p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("\\Qx.y\\E");
System.out.println(p.matcher("x.y").matches() + " Perl-style"); // true Perl-style quoting

cards.front: Which escape form matches one Unicode code point like the Han character for east?
cards.extra: The \u form takes exactly four hex digits; the Perl \x{...} form is flexible, so it is the only way to write code points above U+FFFF.
cards.example:
var u = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("\\u6771").matcher("東").find();
var x = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("\\x{6771}").matcher("東").find();
System.out.println(u + " " + x); // true true

cards.front: What does \p{prop} match, and what does the capital \P{prop} match?
cards.back: \p: char in the property; \P: char not in it
cards.extra: Properties are checked per character, so \p{IsL}\p{IsL}+ style sequences compose a word-run match over Unicode letters.
cards.example:
System.out.println("A".matches("\\p{Lu}")); // true: in the property
System.out.println("A".matches("\\P{Lu}")); // false: uppercase letter is excluded
System.out.println("a".matches("\\P{Lu}")); // true: not in the property

cards.front: Which three kinds of Unicode property can \p{...} test?
cards.extra: Scripts are written \p{IsHiragana} or \p{script=Hiragana}, blocks \p{InMongolian} or \p{block=Mongolian}.
cards.example:
System.out.println("A".matches("\\p{IsLatin}"));      // script
System.out.println("A".matches("\\p{InBasicLatin}")); // block
System.out.println("A".matches("\\p{Lu}"));           // general category

cards.front: Which two keywords/long forms name a Unicode general category in a regex?
cards.extra: Prefixing with Is also works, e.g. \p{IsL} for letters. The categories follow the Unicode Standard version used by java.lang.Character.
cards.example:
System.out.println("A".matches("\\p{gc=Lu}"));               // true: short category form
System.out.println("A".matches("\\p{general_category=Lu}")); // true: long form

cards.front: Since which JDK release has Java regex supported Unicode (version 6.0) features?
cards.extra: Before that, \p{...} existed but the supported property set was narrower and Unicode-aware case folding needed extra care.
cards.example:
// As of JDK 7, regex supports Unicode 6.0 (Oracle Java Tutorials).
System.out.println("A".matches("\\p{IsLatin}")); // Unicode script property works

cards.front: A regex match spans indices 0 to 3 on "foo". Is the end index inclusive or exclusive?
cards.back: Exclusive - the range is start inclusive, end exclusive
cards.extra: The string occupies cells 0, 1, 2 and the index positions sit between cells, so the end index is the position after the last matched character.
cards.example:
var m = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("foo").matcher("foo");
System.out.println(m.find() + " " + m.start() + " " + m.end()); // true 0 3 (end excluded)

cards.front: What is a regex metacharacter?
cards.back: A character the matcher treats as having special meaning, not a literal
cards.extra: In cat. the dot matches the 's' of 'cats' because '.' means any character, which is why literal dots must be escaped.
cards.example:
System.out.println("a.c".matches("a.c"));  // true: . is a metacharacter
System.out.println("a.c".matches("a\\.c")); // true: escaped . is a literal

cards.front: Which characters are the regex metacharacters in the Java API?
cards.extra: This is the complete documented set. Characters outside it, such as @ and #, are never metacharacters and never need quoting.
cards.example:
String meta = "<([{\\^-=$!|]})?*+."; // the Java API metacharacters
System.out.println(meta); // printed as-is: <([{\^-=$!|]})?*+.

cards.front: What are the two ways to force a metacharacter to be treated as an ordinary character?
cards.back: Precede it with a backslash, or wrap it in \Q...\E
cards.extra: The quoting pair can be placed anywhere in the expression as long as \Q comes first, which makes it handy for embedding an arbitrary runtime string.
cards.example:
var slash = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("\\.").matcher(".").matches();
var quoted = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("\\Q.\\E").matcher(".").matches();
System.out.println(slash + " " + quoted); // true true

cards.front: In a Java string literal you want the regex \d. What must you write?
cards.extra: The extra backslash is consumed by Java string escaping, so only one reaches the regex engine. Text read from the console needs no doubling.
cards.example:
String regex = "\\d"; // two backslashes in the Java string literal
System.out.println("5".matches(regex)); // true: the regex is \d

cards.front: In regex terminology, what is a character class?
cards.back: A set of characters in square brackets that matches one character from the set
cards.extra: It is unrelated to Java classes in your source code. [abc] matches exactly one of a, b or c, so [bcr]at matches bat, cat or rat.
cards.example:
var p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("[bcr]at");
System.out.println(p.matcher("rat").matches() + " " + p.matcher("sat").matches()); // true false

cards.front: How do you negate a character class so it matches anything but the listed characters?
cards.back: Put ^ immediately after the opening bracket: [^abc]
cards.extra: Negation still consumes exactly one character; it fails only on the characters inside the class.
cards.example:
var p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("[^abc]");
System.out.println(p.matcher("d").matches() + " " + p.matcher("a").matches()); // true false

cards.front: How do you express the range 'a through z, or A through Z' in one character class?
cards.back: [a-zA-Z] - ranges sit side by side inside the brackets
cards.extra: The hyphen between two characters means an inclusive range. Outside brackets, or after a leading/trailing position, it is a literal hyphen.
cards.example:
System.out.println("q".matches("[a-zA-Z]")); // true: lowercase range
System.out.println("Q".matches("[a-zA-Z]")); // true: uppercase range
System.out.println("5".matches("[a-zA-Z]")); // false: not a letter

cards.front: How do you build a union of two character classes?
cards.back: Nest one class inside the other: [0-4[6-8]]
cards.extra: A union collects all members, so the example matches 0-4 and 6-8 but not 5. Equivalent shorthand is [0-46-8].
cards.example:
var p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("[0-4[6-8]]");
System.out.println(p.matcher("3").matches() + " " + p.matcher("7").matches() + " " + p.matcher("5").matches()); // true true false

cards.front: What operator builds the intersection of two nested classes?
cards.extra: The result keeps only characters present in every nested class, so the example matches 3, 4 and 5 only.
cards.example:
var p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("[0-5&&[3-9]]");
System.out.println(p.matcher("4").matches() + " " + p.matcher("7").matches()); // true false

cards.front: Which expression matches the digits 0-9 except 3, 4 and 5?
cards.extra: This is subtraction: intersect all digits with the complement of the excluded set. [a-z&&[^m-p]] is the letter equivalent.
cards.example:
var p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("[0-9&&[^345]]");
System.out.println(p.matcher("7").matches() + " " + p.matcher("4").matches()); // true false

cards.front: In a character class, what is the difference between [a-d[m-p]] and [a-d&&[m-p]]?
cards.back: The first is a union (a-d plus m-p); the second is an intersection
cards.extra: Nesting without an operator adds the sets, joining them with && keeps only the shared members, which here do not overlap.
cards.example:
System.out.println("m".matches("[a-d[m-p]]"));   // true: union of a-d and m-p
System.out.println("m".matches("[a-d&&[m-p]]")); // false: disjoint ranges have empty intersection

cards.front: What exactly does \s match?
cards.back: [ \t\n\x0B\f\r] - space, tab, newline, VT, FF, CR
cards.extra: It is a shorthand class, not 'any whitespace in every charset'. \S is the complement.
cards.example:
// \s = [ \t\n\x0B\f\r]
System.out.println(" \t\n\u000B\f\r".matches("\\s{6}")); // true: all six whitespace characters

cards.front: Which characters does \w match?
cards.extra: Only ASCII by default, so accented and non-Latin letters are non-word characters; \W matches the complement.
cards.example:
System.out.println("a_9".matches("[a-zA-Z_0-9]+")); // true: letters, underscore, digits
System.out.println("a_9".matches("\\w+"));          // true: \w covers the same characters

cards.front: By default, does the dot . match a line terminator?
cards.back: . does not match line terminators by default; Pattern.DOTALL makes it match
cards.extra: In practice the dot excludes line terminators unless DOTALL mode (?s) is enabled; \n must then be matched explicitly or via DOTALL.
cards.example:
var s = "a\nb";
var plain = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("a.b").matcher(s).find();
var dotall = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("a.b", java.util.regex.Pattern.DOTALL).matcher(s).find();
System.out.println(plain + " " + dotall); // false true - dot skips line terminators by default

cards.front: What does the capital letter form of a predefined class mean?
cards.extra: The rule holds uniformly across the predefined classes, so once you know the lowercase meaning the uppercase follows.
cards.example:
var lower = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("\\d\\s\\w").matcher("1 a").matches();
var upper = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("\\D\\S\\W").matcher("a1!").matches();
System.out.println(lower + " " + upper); // true true: capitals are the opposite sets

cards.front: Why prefer \d or \w over writing [0-9] or [a-zA-Z_0-9] by hand?
cards.back: Better readability and fewer errors from malformed character classes
cards.extra: Hand-built classes invite mistakes such as a misplaced hyphen. The predefined forms are also what most developers recognise at a glance.
cards.example:
System.out.println("12345".matches("[0-9]+")); // true, but hand-written class
System.out.println("12345".matches("\\d+"));   // true: \d is shorter, fewer typos

cards.front: Write an exact count of n in greedy, reluctant and possessive form.
cards.extra: Appending ? makes a quantifier reluctant, appending + makes it possessive. The base forms are ?, *, +, {n}, {n,}, {n,m}.
cards.example:
System.out.println("XXX".matches("X{3}"));  // true: greedy
System.out.println("XXX".matches("X{3}?")); // true: reluctant
System.out.println("XXX".matches("X{3}+")); // true: possessive

cards.front: What is a zero-length match?
cards.back: A match where start and end indices are equal, consuming no characters
cards.extra: It happens in an empty input, at the beginning or end of the input, or between any two characters - anywhere a quantifier permitting zero occurrences fires.
cards.example:
java.util.regex.Matcher m = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("a*").matcher("b");
while (m.find()) System.out.println(m.start() + "==" + m.end()); // 0==0, 1==1: zero-length

cards.front: Does the quantifier in abc+ apply to the whole sequence 'abc'?
cards.back: No - it applies to c only: a, then b, then c one or more times
cards.extra: Quantifiers bind to one character, one character class, or one group. Use (abc)+ to repeat the whole sequence.
cards.example:
System.out.println("abc".matches("abc+"));   // true: c once
System.out.println("abcc".matches("abc+"));  // true: only c repeats
System.out.println("abcabc".matches("abc+")); // false: abc as a whole does not repeat

cards.front: What does a greedy quantifier do before its first match attempt?
cards.back: Eats the entire input, then backtracks one character at a time
cards.extra: .*foo on xfooxxxxxxfoo first consumes everything, then backs off until the rightmost 'foo' is restored.
cards.example:
var m = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("a.*b").matcher("a1b2b");
m.find();
System.out.println(m.group() + " " + m.start() + " " + m.end()); // a1b2b 0 5

cards.front: How does a reluctant quantifier search?
cards.back: Starts with the shortest match and grows one character at a time
cards.extra: Reluctant .*?foo finds the leftmost 'foo' first, then continues scanning, so it yields both occurrences in xfooxxxxxxfoo.
cards.example:
var s = "a1b2b";
var greedy = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("a.*b").matcher(s);
var rel = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("a.*?b").matcher(s);
greedy.find(); rel.find();
System.out.println(greedy.group() + " " + rel.group()); // a1b2b a1b

cards.front: What distinguishes a possessive quantifier from a greedy one?
cards.back: It never backtracks - it tries once with the whole input and gives up
cards.extra: .*+foo on xfooxxxxxxfoo fails, because .*+ consumes everything and leaves nothing for 'foo'.
cards.example:
var g = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("a*a").matcher("aaa").matches();
var ps = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("a*+a").matcher("aaa").matches();
System.out.println(g + " " + ps); // true false: possessive never backtracks

cards.front: Why use a possessive quantifier such as [0-9]++ instead of a greedy one?
cards.back: Avoids backtracking, so it outperforms greedy when no match is found immediately
cards.extra: Preventing backtracking also defuses catastrophic backtracking patterns, where nested greedy quantifiers explode exponentially on a failing input.
cards.example:
String s = "99999999999999999999x";
System.out.println(s.matches("[0-9]++x"));  // true: possessive takes the digits once
System.out.println(s.matches("[0-9]++y"));  // false: possessive never backtracks
// [0-9]+y would retry every shorter digit prefix first.

cards.front: Which quantifiers match zero occurrences and therefore produce a zero-length match after the last character?
cards.extra: On input 'aaaaa', a? matches each 'a' then a zero-length match at index 5, whereas a+ stops after the run.
cards.example:
for (String re : new String[] {"a?", "a*"}) {
    java.util.regex.Matcher m = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile(re).matcher("b");
    while (m.find()) System.out.println(re + " " + m.start() + ".." + m.end()); // 0..0, 1..1
}

cards.front: Matching a? against 'ababaaaab' reports a zero-length match at each 'b'. Why?
cards.back: a? only asks whether an 'a' is present, and zero 'a' satisfies it
cards.extra: Any position not followed by 'a' matches the empty alternative, so non-'a' characters appear as zero-length matches rather than failures.
cards.example:
java.util.regex.Matcher m = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("a?").matcher("ababaaaab");
while (m.find())
    if (m.end() == m.start()) System.out.println(m.start()); // 1, 3, 8 (b's), then 9 (end)

cards.front: Which quantifier means 'at least n but not more than m'?
cards.extra: Reluctant and possessive variants are X{n,m}? and X{n,m}+. A comma alone after n (X{n,}) means 'at least n' with no upper limit.
cards.example:
System.out.println("XXX".matches("X{2,4}"));  // true: at least 2, at most 4
System.out.println("X".matches("X{2,4}"));    // false: fewer than the minimum

cards.front: Which boundary matcher matches the end of the input, ignoring a final line terminator?
cards.extra: \z is the strict end of input. The HALT distinction matters when a file ends with a trailing newline.
cards.example:
java.util.regex.Matcher m = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("abc\\Z").matcher("abc\n");
System.out.println(m.find() + " " + m.end()); // true 3: \Z matches before the final line terminator

cards.front: Which boundary matchers anchor to the start and end of a line?
cards.back: ^ for start of line, $ for end of line
cards.extra: Without MULTILINE mode they only match at the beginning and end of the whole input; \A and \z always mean the absolute input limits.
cards.example:
var p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("^dog$", java.util.regex.Pattern.MULTILINE);
System.out.println(p.matcher("cat\ndog\nbird").find()); // true: ^ and $ anchor each line

cards.front: How do you match the word 'dog' only as a whole word, not inside a longer word?
cards.extra: A word boundary is a transition between a word character (\w) and a non-word character or the input edge.
cards.example:
var p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("\\bdog\\b");
System.out.println(p.matcher("a dog").find() + " " + p.matcher("dogmatic").find()); // true false

cards.front: What does \B match in Java regex?
cards.back: A non-word boundary - a position that is not a word boundary
cards.extra: A position is not a word boundary where word characters continue across it. Note confusing - the reliable use is matching inside a word, where \b would fail.
cards.example:
var p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("\\B");
var m = p.matcher("ab");
System.out.println(m.find() + " " + m.start()); // true 1

cards.front: Which boundary matcher anchors a match to the end of the previous match?
cards.extra: It makes repeated find() calls contiguous, so a second occurrence of the target that does not start where the last match ended is skipped.
cards.example:
var m = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("\\Gdog").matcher("dog dog");
System.out.println(m.find() + " " + m.find()); // true false: only at end of previous match

cards.front: How are capturing groups numbered in a pattern?
cards.back: By counting opening parentheses from left to right
cards.extra: In ((A)(B(C))) group 1 is the outer group, 2 is (A), 3 is (B(C)) and 4 is (C).
cards.example:
var m = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("((a)(b))").matcher("ab");
m.matches();
System.out.println(m.group(1) + " " + m.group(2) + " " + m.group(3)); // ab a b

cards.front: Does groupCount() include group 0?
cards.back: No - group 0 is the entire match and is not counted
cards.extra: So ((A)(B(C))) reports 4. group(0) still returns the whole matched text.
cards.example:
java.util.regex.Matcher m = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("(a)(b)").matcher("ab");
m.find(); // true
System.out.println(m.groupCount() + " " + m.group()); // 2 ab: group 0 is not counted

cards.front: Which groups do not count toward groupCount()?
cards.extra: Writing (?:dog) groups for quantification without capturing, which keeps the numbering of the remaining groups stable.
cards.example:
var p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("(a)(?:b)(c)");
var m = p.matcher("abc");
m.find();
System.out.println(p.matcher("abc").groupCount() + " " + m.group(2)); // 2 c

cards.front: What does start(int group) return?
cards.back: The start index of the subsequence captured by that group in the previous match
cards.extra: start() with no argument returns the start of the whole match; end(g) returns the index of the last character plus one.
cards.example:
var m = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("(a)(b)").matcher("zab");
m.find();
System.out.println(m.start(1) + " " + m.start(2) + " " + m.group(2)); // 1 2 b

cards.front: What does end(int group) return?
cards.back: The index of the last character plus one captured by that group
cards.extra: That is the exclusive end offset, matching String.substring(start, end). group(g) returns the captured text itself.
cards.example:
java.util.regex.Matcher m = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("(a+)(b+)").matcher("xaaabb");
System.out.println(m.find()); // true
System.out.println(m.end(1) + " " + m.end(2)); // 4 6: index after each group's last char

cards.front: Write a backreference to capture group 1 inside the pattern.
cards.back: \1 - a backslash followed by the group number
cards.extra: (\d\d)\1 matches any two digits followed by the identical two digits, and fails if the last two digits differ.
cards.example:
var p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("(\\w+)-\\1");
System.out.println(p.matcher("go-go").find() + " " + p.matcher("go-stop").find()); // true false

cards.front: What does a backreference match?
cards.back: The exact text already captured by the referenced group, not just its pattern
cards.extra: So (\d\d)\1 accepts '1212' but rejects '1234', which a repeated \d\d\d\d would accept.
cards.example:
var p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("(\\w+)\\s+\\1");
System.out.println(p.matcher("hi hi").find() + " " + p.matcher("hi bye").find()); // true false

cards.front: Which Pattern flag makes . also match line terminators?
cards.extra: The 's' is a mnemonic for 'single-line' mode as it is called in Perl, which is why the letter does not match the flag name.
cards.example:
java.util.regex.Pattern p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("a.b", java.util.regex.Pattern.DOTALL); // (?s)
System.out.println("a\nb".matches("a.b"));   // false: . does not match a line terminator
System.out.println(p.matcher("a\nb").matches()); // true: DOTALL makes . match it

cards.front: Which Pattern flag makes ^ and $ match at line terminators?
cards.extra: By default those anchors only match at the start and end of the entire input sequence.
cards.example:
java.util.regex.Pattern p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("^b$", java.util.regex.Pattern.MULTILINE); // (?m)
System.out.println(p.matcher("a\nb").find());  // true: ^ and $ match at the line terminator
System.out.println(java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("^b$").matcher("a\nb").find()); // false without the flag

cards.front: Which Pattern flag lets a pattern contain whitespace and # comments?
cards.extra: Whitespace is ignored and # comments run to end of line, which enables readable multi-line patterns for parsing tasks.
cards.example:
java.util.regex.Pattern p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("a # comment\n b", java.util.regex.Pattern.COMMENTS);
System.out.println(p.matcher("ab").matches()); // true: whitespace and # text ignored
java.util.regex.Pattern q = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("(?x)a # comment\n b");
System.out.println(q.matcher("ab").matches()); // true: embedded (?x) is the same flag

cards.front: Which Pattern flag treats the entire pattern as literal text?
cards.extra: Metacharacters and escape sequences lose their meaning. Only CASE_INSENSITIVE and UNICODE_CASE still apply alongside it.
cards.example:
java.util.regex.Pattern p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("a.c", java.util.regex.Pattern.LITERAL); // no embedded form
System.out.println(p.matcher("a.c").matches()); // true
System.out.println(p.matcher("abc").matches()); // false: dot is literal text

cards.front: What does Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE do on its own, and what must you add for Unicode?
cards.back: Only US-ASCII case folding; add UNICODE_CASE for Unicode-aware folding
cards.extra: The embedded equivalent pair is (?iu). Without it, Ä and ä differ as far as the matcher is concerned.
cards.example:
var ascii = java.util.regex.Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE;
var unicode = ascii | java.util.regex.Pattern.UNICODE_CASE;
var re = "é";
System.out.println(java.util.regex.Pattern.compile(re, ascii).matcher("É").matches() + " " + java.util.regex.Pattern.compile(re, unicode).matcher("É").matches()); // false true

cards.front: Which constant/embedded flag pair enables Unix lines mode?
cards.extra: In that mode only \n counts as a line terminator for ., ^ and $, which matters when files contain \r.
cards.example:
java.util.regex.Pattern p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("a.b", java.util.regex.Pattern.UNIX_LINES); // (?d)
System.out.println(p.matcher("a\nb").matches() + " " + p.matcher("a\rb").matches()); // false true: only \n is a terminator

cards.front: Which Pattern flags have no embedded flag expression?
cards.extra: Every other flag has a letter: (?i) case-insensitive, (?x) comments, (?m) multiline, (?s) dotall, (?u) Unicode case, (?d) Unix lines.
cards.example:
int flags = java.util.regex.Pattern.CANON_EQ | java.util.regex.Pattern.LITERAL;
java.util.regex.Pattern p = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("a.b", flags);
System.out.println(p.matcher("a.b").matches()); // LITERAL: the dot is a dot
// CANON_EQ and LITERAL have no (?...) embedded flag form

cards.front: What does Pattern.CANON_EQ change about matching?
cards.back: Two characters match only if their full canonical decompositions match
cards.extra: a\u030A then matches \u00E5. It is disabled by default and can impose a performance penalty.
cards.example:
System.out.println(java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("\u00E9").matcher("e\u0301").matches()); // false without CANON_EQ
System.out.println(java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("\u00E9", java.util.regex.Pattern.CANON_EQ)
    .matcher("e\u0301").matches()); // true: decompositions match

cards.front: How do you combine several Pattern flags in one compile call?
cards.extra: The flags parameter is an int bit mask, so the flags compose. The embedded alternative chains the letters, e.g. (?im).
cards.example:
var re = "^DOG$";
var flags = java.util.regex.Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE | java.util.regex.Pattern.MULTILINE;
System.out.println(java.util.regex.Pattern.compile(re, flags).matcher("cat\ndog").find()); // true

cards.front: What does Pattern.matches(regex, input) return for "\\d" and "1"?
cards.back: true - the whole input must match the pattern
cards.extra: It is a convenience for compile-match over the entire string, so Pattern.matches("\\d", "12") is false.
cards.example:
System.out.println(java.util.regex.Pattern.matches("\\d", "1"));  // true: whole input matches
System.out.println(java.util.regex.Pattern.matches("\\d", "a1")); // false: a1 does not

cards.front: How does Pattern.split() treat trailing empty strings?
cards.back: With the no-limit form they are discarded
cards.extra: "one:two:".split(":") returns two elements. Passing a limit of zero gives the same result; a negative limit keeps trailing empties.
cards.example:
String[] a = "a,b,".split(",");     // [a, b]: trailing empty discarded
String[] b = "a,b,".split(",", -1); // [a, b, ]: limit keeps it
System.out.println(a.length + " " + b.length); // 2 3

cards.front: What does Pattern.quote(s) return?
cards.back: A literal pattern string that matches s exactly
cards.extra: Metacharacters and escapes in s get no special meaning, making it safe to interpolate untrusted text into a larger pattern such as a split delimiter.
cards.example:
String lit = java.util.regex.Pattern.quote("a.c");
System.out.println(lit); // \Qa.c\E: a literal pattern string
System.out.println("a.c".matches(lit)); // true: matches the original text exactly

cards.front: Are Pattern.CANON_EQ and Pattern.LITERAL available as embedded flags like (?i)?
cards.back: No - neither has an embedded flag expression
cards.extra: Both must be passed to the two-argument compile. Trying to write them inline produces a dangling-metacharacter syntax error.
cards.example:
System.out.println(java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("(?i)a").matcher("A").matches()); // true: (?i) exists
// Neither LITERAL nor CANON_EQ has an embedded (?...) form.
// Use Pattern.compile(s, Pattern.LITERAL) or Pattern.compile(s, Pattern.CANON_EQ).

cards.front: What does str.replace("aa", "b") do on "aaa"?
cards.back: Returns "ba" - replacement runs left to right, non-overlapping
cards.extra: The second 'a' is left unmatched because the scan continues after the replaced span, so 'aa' at index 0 wins over 'aa' at index 1.
cards.example:
String s = "aaa".replace("aa", "b");
System.out.println(s); // ba: left to right, non-overlapping

cards.front: Which Matcher methods return the positions of the previous match?
cards.extra: They are the index methods. end() is the offset after the last character matched, i.e. an exclusive end position.
cards.example:
var m = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("(a)(b)").matcher("zab");
m.find();
System.out.println(m.start() + " " + m.end() + " " + m.start(1) + " " + m.end(2)); // 1 3 1 3

cards.front: matches() vs lookingAt(): what is the difference?
cards.extra: Both always start at the beginning of the region. find() is the one that scans forward for a match anywhere in the input.
cards.example:
System.out.println(java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("\\d+").matcher("123abc").matches());   // false: entire region required
System.out.println(java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("\\d+").matcher("123abc").lookingAt()); // true: prefix is enough

cards.front: Which Matcher method finds the next matching subsequence anywhere in the input?
cards.extra: Repeated calls continue from the end of the previous match, which is the usual way to iterate all matches in a loop.
cards.example:
var m = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("dog").matcher("a dog, another dog");
System.out.println(m.find() + " " + m.find()); // true true - next subsequence anywhere

cards.front: Which Matcher method resets the matcher and matches again starting from an explicit index?
cards.extra: It first resets the matcher, so any prior match state is discarded before scanning from the given index.
cards.example:
java.util.regex.Matcher m = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("\\d+").matcher("a1b22c333");
System.out.println(m.find(5) + " " + m.group()); // true 333: reset, start searching at index 5

cards.front: Which Matcher method replaces every match and returns the new string?
cards.extra: replaceFirst replaces only the first match. Both return a new String; the matcher's input is unchanged.
cards.example:
java.util.regex.Matcher m = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("\\d+").matcher("a1b22");
System.out.println(m.replaceAll("#")); // a#b#: every match replaced

cards.front: Why call Matcher.quoteReplacement(s) before using s as a replacement?
cards.back: In a replacement string the special character is the backslash (\\), and $ introduces a group reference — not the slash
cards.extra: It escapes \ and $ so the text is used literally. Otherwise a group reference like $1 in the text would be substituted instead.
cards.example:
var s = "$1\\x";
var out = "x".replaceAll("x", java.util.regex.Matcher.quoteReplacement(s));
System.out.println(out); // $1\x - backslash and $ stay literal

cards.front: Which two Matcher methods perform a manual append-and-replace loop?
cards.extra: appendReplacement is the non-terminal step inside the loop, appendTail is the terminal step that copies the remainder after the last match.
cards.example:
java.util.regex.Matcher m = java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("cat").matcher("cat dog cat");
StringBuffer sb = new StringBuffer();
while (m.find()) m.appendReplacement(sb, "fox");
m.appendTail(sb);
System.out.println(sb); // fox dog fox

cards.front: str.replaceAll(regex, repl) vs str.replace(target, repl) - what is the difference?
cards.extra: That is why a string containing regex metacharacters such as '.' or '$' behaves unpredictably with replaceAll but safely with replace.
cards.example:
System.out.println("a.c".replaceAll(".", "X")); // XXX: the target is a regex
System.out.println("a.c".replace(".", "X"));    // aXc: the target is literal text

cards.front: Which method of PatternSyntaxException returns the index where the error occurred?
cards.extra: Sibling methods are getDescription() for the reason and getPattern() for the offending expression.
cards.example:
try { java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("[a-"); } catch (java.util.regex.PatternSyntaxException e) {
    System.out.println("index " + e.getIndex()); // index of the error in the pattern
}

cards.front: What does PatternSyntaxException.getMessage() produce?
cards.back: A multi-line string: description, index, the pattern, and a caret marking the index
cards.extra: The caret line is the useful part when logging: it points at the exact character the parser choked on.
cards.example:
try { java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("[a-"); } catch (java.util.regex.PatternSyntaxException e) {
    System.out.println(e.getMessage()); // description, index, pattern, caret on separate lines
}

cards.front: Typing ?i)foo instead of (?i)foo throws what, at which index?
cards.extra: The parser sees the question mark as a quantifier with nothing to quantify and reports index 0, not the missing parenthesis. getIndex() gives the same number.
cards.example:
try { java.util.regex.Pattern.compile("?i)foo"); }
catch (java.util.regex.PatternSyntaxException e) { System.out.println(e.getIndex() + " " + e.getDescription()); }
// 0 Dangling meta character '?\'

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: What does a Java garbage collector periodically do in three steps?
cards.back: Check reachability, remove unreachable objects, then reorganize survivors
cards.extra: Reorganizing live objects compactly is what makes later collections cheaper, and it is something manual free/delete in C++ never does.
cards.example:
String[] steps = {"check reachability", "remove unreachable objects", "reorganize survivors"};
for (String step : steps) System.out.println(step);

cards.front: Which two concrete costs does manual memory management trade for its control?
cards.back: Developers must know how memory is used and hand-write alloc/free control code
cards.extra: That control code obscures the business logic, and a missed error path becomes a memory leak - the exact class of bug the GC exists to prevent.
cards.example:
byte[] block = new byte[16]; // manual management: you hand-write the allocation
// you must know how memory is used and write the matching free code
System.out.println(block.length); // Java does this bookkeeping for you

cards.front: Does garbage collection eliminate memory leaks completely?
cards.back: No - it vastly reduces but does not eliminate them
cards.extra: Leaks still happen through lingering references: static collections that grow forever, listeners never deregistered, or ThreadLocal values kept by pool threads.
cards.example:
java.util.List<Object> listeners = new java.util.ArrayList<>();
listeners.add(new Object());
listeners.add(new Object()); // reachable references: GC cannot collect them
System.out.println(listeners.size()); // leaks can remain

cards.front: In Java, does null-ing a local variable make its object collectible immediately?
cards.back: No - unreachability is decided by the collector, not by assignment order
cards.extra: A local reference stops making its object reachable when the scope ends; the collector then frees it at its own convenience.
cards.example:
Object obj = new Object();
obj = null; // no immediate collection: the GC, not assignment order, decides reachability
System.out.println(obj == null); // true here, but the object may still be alive

cards.front: What does the weak generational hypothesis state?
cards.extra: Generational collectors bet on it: scanning the young generation finds most garbage, so CPU time is spent where collection pays off.
cards.example:
Object shortLived = new Object(); // most objects are short-lived
shortLived = null;                // unreachable soon after allocation
System.out.println(shortLived == null); // true

cards.front: Which two JVM arguments set the initial/minimum and maximum heap size?
cards.back: -Xms for initial and minimum, -Xmx for maximum
cards.extra: Both take a size with a k/m/g suffix. If the heap is exhausted, the JVM throws java.lang.OutOfMemoryError on the next allocation.
cards.example:
String minHeap = "-Xms";
String maxHeap = "-Xmx";
System.out.println(minHeap + " = initial/minimum heap; " + maxHeap + " = maximum heap");

cards.front: In a generational collector, where is a new object allocated?
cards.back: Eden space - part of the young generation
cards.extra: After it survives a collection it is copied to a survivor space; surviving enough collections moves it to the old generation.
cards.example:
Object obj = new Object();   // new objects are allocated in Eden, part of the young generation
String region = "Eden";
System.out.println(region + ": " + obj.getClass().getSimpleName());

cards.front: What is stored in the permanent / metaspace region?
cards.back: JVM metadata and core system classes that live for the JVM's lifetime
cards.extra: It is not ordinary application data: classes, method metadata and similar long-lived structures land there, not new objects.
cards.example:
class PermanentRegion {
    String contents = "JVM metadata and core system classes"; // live for the JVM's lifetime
}

cards.front: What does an evacuating garbage collector do?
cards.back: Finds live objects and copies them to a new region; old regions become free
cards.extra: The name is counter-intuitive: it does not hunt for garbage, it salvages survivors, and whole regions are reclaimed once drained.
cards.example:
String action = "copy live objects to a new region";
String result = "old region becomes free";
System.out.println(action + "; " + result);

cards.front: What does an incremental garbage collector do with the heap?
cards.back: Divides it into many small regions of a few MB instead of one young/old space
cards.extra: Smaller units let the collector work on a few regions at a time, which shortens pauses and avoids managing one monolithic heap.
cards.example:
String layout = "many small regions of a few MB"; // incremental collector
boolean oneYoungOldSpace = false;
System.out.println(layout + ", not one young/old space: " + oneYoungOldSpace);

cards.front: Which objects serve as GC roots?
cards.back: Local variables, static class fields, active threads, JNI references
cards.extra: Marking starts only from roots and traverses the object graph, so anything not reachable from a root is collected.
cards.example:
class Ex {
  static Object staticField = new Object();
  void m(Object jniRef) {
    Object local = new Object();
    Thread active = Thread.currentThread();
    System.out.println(local + " " + staticField + " " + active + " " + jniRef);
  }
}

cards.front: What marking value does the VM give each object, and what does the mark phase do?
cards.back: A 1-bit flag initially false; marking sets it true for reachable objects
cards.extra: The collector traverses the object graph from the roots and flips the bit for everything it can reach, rather than scanning objects blindly.
cards.example:
boolean marked = false; // the VM marking bit starts false (0)
Object reachable = new Object();
marked = true;          // marking sets the bit of reachable objects
System.out.println(marked && reachable != null); // true

cards.front: What happens during the sweep phase?
cards.back: All objects whose mark bit is still false are removed
cards.extra: Sweeping follows marking, so the mark bit alone decides liveness - no per-object reference counting is involved.
cards.example:
boolean markBit = false;
if (!markBit) System.out.println("removed during sweep");

cards.front: What is a minor garbage collection?
cards.back: A collection that scans only the young generations
cards.extra: Minor collections are frequent and cheap. A major collection also scans the old generation and is usually triggered by a heap-occupancy threshold.
cards.example:
Object young = new Object(); // fresh object: young generation
Object old = new Object();   // survivor promoted to old generation
System.out.println(young != old);
// a minor collection scans only the young generations

cards.front: What is a major garbage collection?
cards.back: A collection that scans young and old generations
cards.extra: Much rarer than a minor collection, and typically triggered by a condition such as a threshold percentage of heap memory being used.
cards.example:
String major = "major garbage collection";
System.out.println(major + " scans young and old generations");

cards.front: In GC terminology, what does concurrent mean?
cards.back: GC work runs while the application runs
cards.extra: It narrows pauses at the cost of throughput. Parallel means GC work uses several cores; concurrent means application threads keep running during GC.
cards.example:
Thread app = new Thread(() -> System.out.println("application work"));
Thread gc = new Thread(() -> System.out.println("GC work")); // concurrent: both run
app.start(); gc.start();

cards.front: In GC terminology, what does parallel mean?
cards.extra: G1, Parallel and ZGC are all parallel collectors. Coordinating the work lowers wall-clock GC time but raises overall CPU usage.
cards.example:
int cores = Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors();
System.out.println(cores);   // a parallel collector uses multiple CPU cores

cards.front: What is a stop-the-world event?
cards.back: A pause where all application threads stop for GC work
cards.extra: Heap objects are not thread-safe, so mutation must be frozen while the collector marks, moves or frees objects. JFR and VisualVM measure pause duration.
cards.example:
var threads = Thread.getAllStackTraces().keySet();
System.out.println(threads.size());
// stop-the-world: all application threads stop while the collector works

cards.front: Which GC was the default since JDK 9, and which was removed in JDK 14?
cards.extra: CMS was deprecated in JDK 9 and deleted in JDK 14; G1 was built as its replacement with more consistent pause times.
cards.example:
System.out.println("G1: default since JDK 9");
System.out.println("CMS: removed in JDK 14");

cards.front: In G1, what makes an object humongous?
cards.back: It is larger than half a region
cards.extra: Such an object gets one or more contiguous regions of its own, bypasses eden and survivor, and is treated like an old-gen object from the start.
cards.example:
String threshold = "half a region";
System.out.println("G1 humongous object: larger than " + threshold);

cards.front: What are G1's two top-level GC cycle phases?
cards.extra: G1 starts in Young-Only; when old-gen occupancy crosses a threshold it runs the concurrent marking trio and then mixed collections.
cards.example:
String[] phases = {"Young-Only", "Space-Reclamation"}; // in this order
for (String phase : phases) System.out.println(phase);

cards.front: Name the three special pauses of G1's concurrent marking phase, in order.
cards.extra: Concurrent Start still evacuates young regions; Remark and Cleanup do not. Between them G1 finalises marking, unloads classes, and reclaims empty regions.
cards.example:
String[] pauses = {"Concurrent Start", "Remark", "Cleanup"};
for (String pause : pauses) System.out.println(pause);

cards.front: Which G1 pause finalises marking and performs class unloading?
cards.extra: It also does reference processing and frees empty regions; no young evacuation happens during this pause.
cards.example:
String pause = "Remark";       // finalizes marking
boolean classUnloading = true; // and performs class unloading
System.out.println(pause + ": " + classUnloading);

cards.front: What is a mixed collection in G1?
cards.back: A collection that evacuates young and selected old regions
cards.extra: Mixed collections run through the Space-Reclamation phase; the old regions chosen are the ones with the most garbage.
cards.example:
boolean evacuateYoung = true;
boolean evacuateSelectedOld = true; // mixed collection: young and selected old regions
System.out.println(evacuateYoung);
System.out.println(evacuateSelectedOld);

cards.front: Why is the collector called Garbage-First?
cards.back: It reclaims the old regions with the most garbage first
cards.extra: An efficiency algorithm ranks regions by reclaimable space, so emptying a mostly-garbage region frees the most memory per unit of pause time.
cards.example:
String collector = "Garbage-First";
String policy = "reclaim old regions with the most garbage first";
System.out.println(collector + ": " + policy);

cards.front: Which condition made the JVM choose G1 between JDK 9 and JDK 26?
cards.back: Two or more CPU cores and more than 1792 MB of available memory
cards.extra: Otherwise SerialGC was selected. As of JDK 27 G1 is the default on every configuration and -XX:+UseG1GC is unnecessary.
cards.example:
# JDK 9..26: G1 chosen with 2+ CPU cores and more than 1792 MB memory
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep UseG1GC   # inspect the selection

cards.front: On JDK 8, what is the default collector and what must you pass to use G1?
cards.extra: G1 was experimental in JDK 6u14, standard from JDK 7u4, and only became the server default in JDK 9.
cards.example:
java -version             # JDK 8: default collector is ParallelGC
java -XX:+UseG1GC App     # the flag needed to select G1 on JDK 8

cards.front: What is G1's recommended relationship between -Xmx and the expected live set?
cards.back: 25% above the expected live set size
cards.extra: Headroom lets G1 evacuate without pressure; the exact figure depends on the application's allocation behaviour and latency goals.
cards.example:
String liveSet = "expected live set";
System.out.println("-Xmx = " + liveSet + " + 25%");
System.out.println("G1 recommends -Xmx 25% above the expected live set");

cards.front: Is -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis a hard guarantee in G1?
cards.back: No - it is a soft goal the JVM tries to meet
cards.extra: Raising it trades latency for throughput; lowering it usually does the opposite. There is no setting that improves everything at once.
cards.example:
java -XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 App
# 100 ms is a soft goal G1 tries to meet, not a hard guarantee

cards.front: Which optimisation goal distinguishes G1 from ParallelGC and from ZGC?
cards.back: G1 balances both; Parallel maximizes throughput; ZGC minimizes latency
cards.extra: Choosing a collector is choosing a point in the throughput / latency / footprint triangle - no collector wins on all three.
cards.example:
String g1 = "balances both";
String parallel = "maximizes throughput", zgc = "minimizes latency";
System.out.println("G1 " + g1 + "; Parallel " + parallel + "; ZGC " + zgc);

cards.front: Why set -Xms equal to -Xmx together with -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch?
cards.back: Avoids heap resizing and pre-commits pages, cutting early-lifecycle latency
cards.extra: Without AlwaysPreTouch pages are committed lazily as the heap fills, so the early part of a run pays page-fault costs during pauses.
cards.example:
String size = "SAME";
String args = "-Xms" + size + " -Xmx" + size + " -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch";
System.out.println(args + ": no heap resizing, pages pre-committed, less early-lifecycle latency");

cards.front: Which G1 region types form the young generation?
cards.extra: G1 carves the heap into uniform regions and labels each eden, survivor, old or humongous; the labels change between collections.
cards.example:
String[] young = {"Eden", "survivor"};  // G1 young generation regions
for (String region : young) System.out.println(region);

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::01 JVM Internals

cards.front: What heap size range does ZGC support?
cards.extra: Very frequent, low-pause collections that scan only the young regions.
cards.example:
long minHeapMB = 8;
long maxHeapTB = 16;              // ZGC: 8 MB to 16 TB heaps
System.out.println(minHeapMB + " MB to " + maxHeapTB + " TB");

cards.front: Should you use ZGC on a heaps-as-small-as-8-MB single-core box?
cards.back: No - strongly discouraged despite being technically supported
cards.extra: Rare collections that scan both young and old regions, often triggered by a heap threshold.
cards.example:
java -XX:+UseZGC -Xmx8m App   # technically supported down to 8 MB heaps
# strongly discouraged on a single core: ZGC scales up, not down

cards.front: Which ZGC GC-cycle order alternates pauses and concurrent phases, starting the cycle?
cards.back: Mark Start, Concurrent Mark, Mark End, Prepare for Relocation, Relocate Start, Relocate
cards.extra: Three short pauses bracket three concurrent phases, which is why pauses are just synchronization points rather than real work.
cards.example:
String[] cycle = {"Mark Start", "Concurrent Mark", "Mark End", "Prepare for Relocation", "Relocate Start", "Relocate"};
for (String phase : cycle) System.out.println(phase);

cards.front: Why are ZGC pauses independent of live set size?
cards.back: Nearly all work happens concurrently; pauses only flip flags and colors
cards.extra: Heavy work - marking, relocation, reference processing, class unloading, stack scanning - runs alongside the application instead of inside a pause.
cards.example:
Runnable marking = () -> System.out.println("marking while the app runs");
Thread app = new Thread(marking); // ZGC does nearly all work concurrently
app.start();
// pauses only flip flags and colors, so they do not grow with the live set

cards.front: How many metadata bits does a ZGC colored pointer reserve, and how many are in use?
cards.back: 20 reserved, 4 in use as of JDK 19
cards.extra: The remaining 16 are explicitly reserved for future GC features, which is why the design is described as extensible.
cards.example:
int reservedBits = 20;
int usedBits = 4; // as of JDK 19
System.out.println(usedBits + " of " + reservedBits + " colored-pointer metadata bits in use");

cards.front: What does the ZGC Finalizable pointer bit indicate?
cards.back: The object is reachable only through a finalizer
cards.extra: Finalization itself was deprecated for removal in JDK 18 (JEP 421), so this bit tracks a legacy feature.
cards.example:
boolean finalizableBit = true; // ZGC pointer bit: reachable only through a finalizer
System.out.println(finalizableBit);

cards.front: What do the Marked0 and Marked1 pointer bits do?
cards.back: Show the object is marked; ZGC alternates which is 'good' each cycle
cards.extra: Alternating avoids clearing all bits between cycles - flipping which color is current makes the previous cycle's marks stale in one step.
cards.example:
boolean marked0 = true, marked1 = false; // either bit shows the object is marked
boolean goodColor = true;               // ZGC alternates which bit is good
System.out.println(marked0 == goodColor); // true for this cycle

cards.front: What is ZGC's heap multi-mapping?
cards.back: One physical object mapped into three virtual views, one per pointer color
cards.extra: It lets a load barrier resolve an object that moved since the last sync point. A side effect is reported memory usage that looks inflated.
cards.example:
String[] views = {"Marked0", "Marked1", "Remapped"}; // three virtual views
System.out.println(views.length); // one physical object, one view per color

cards.front: A ZGC process reports memory usage larger than the system's physical RAM. Why?
cards.back: Objects are triplicate-addressed in virtual memory, not truly duplicated
cards.extra: Only the 'real' color view holds physical memory; the other two mappings are address-space aliases, so virtual size is the misleading figure.
cards.example:
long physicalCopies = 1; // the object bytes exist once in physical memory
long virtualViews = 3;   // ZGC maps them into three virtual views
System.out.println(virtualViews > physicalCopies); // reported usage can look larger

cards.front: What are load barriers in ZGC?
cards.back: C2-injected code at heap loads that checks and heals pointer color
cards.extra: They take a fast path for the common 'good' color; on a bad color they update the pointer to the object's new location, keeping later loads cheap.
cards.example:
String barrier = "C2-injected code at heap loads";
String effect = "checks and heals pointer color";
System.out.println(barrier + " " + effect);

cards.front: Which component injects ZGC's load barriers?
cards.back: The C2 compiler of the JIT, when classes are parsed
cards.extra: Because barriers are compiled into the code rather than interpreted, the 'good color' fast path costs little; capping C2 or forcing interpreted mode undermines ZGC's assumptions.
cards.example:
Object o = new Object();   // a reference loaded from the heap
// C2, part of the JIT, injects ZGC load barriers when classes are parsed
System.out.println(o != null);

cards.front: How big is a ZGC small region?
cards.extra: Objects up to 1/8 of a region (256 KB) go in a small region. Medium and large regions exist for bigger objects.
cards.example:
int smallRegionKB = 2 * 1024;  // ZGC small region: 2 MB
System.out.println(smallRegionKB / 1024 + " MB");

cards.front: How are ZGC large regions sized?
cards.back: Fitted to the object in 2 MB increments
cards.extra: A 13 MB object occupies a 14 MB large region. Anything too big for a medium region gets its own large region.
cards.example:
int objBytes = 5 * 1024 * 1024;
long step = 2L * 1024 * 1024;
long regionBytes = ((objBytes + step - 1) / step) * step;   // ZGC large region: fitted in 2 MB increments
System.out.println(regionBytes);

cards.front: At which max heap size does ZGC turn medium regions off?
cards.extra: For heaps of at least 1 GB medium regions are 32 MB; smaller heaps step down through 16, 8 and 4 MB before the feature is disabled.
cards.example:
java -XX:+UseZGC -Xmx64m App   # -Xmx below 128 MB
# ZGC medium regions are off; from 128 MB they are 4 MB

cards.front: Which is ZGC's preferred relocation strategy?
cards.extra: In-place relocation is the fallback when no empty region is free, and it forces single-threaded compaction inside the target region, hurting performance.
cards.example:
String strategy = "not-in-place";
System.out.println(strategy + ": move objects into empty regions");

cards.front: Why does a larger heap help ZGC even at the same live set?
cards.back: More free regions allow not-in-place relocation instead of costly in-place compaction
cards.extra: That plus headroom reduces allocation pressure. In-place relocation is the fallback, and its single-threaded compaction is slow.
cards.example:
String heap = "larger heap at the same live set";
System.out.println(heap + " means more free regions");
System.out.println("not-in-place relocation instead of in-place compaction");

cards.front: Which ZGC option sets the maximum heap fragmentation percent, and what is the default?
cards.extra: Lowering it compacts more aggressively, reclaiming memory at the cost of CPU time.
cards.example:
java -XX:+UseZGC App                            # default -XX:ZFragmentationLimit=25
java -XX:+UseZGC -XX:ZFragmentationLimit=10 App  # allow less fragmentation

cards.front: Which ZGC option sets the max interval between cycles, and what is the default?
cards.extra: A non-zero value forces a collection even when the allocation rate would not trigger one, at some throughput cost.
cards.example:
String option = "-XX:ZCollectionInterval"; // max seconds between cycles
int defaultValue = 0;                      // 0 means disabled
System.out.println(option + "=" + defaultValue);

cards.front: What is the default for -XX:ZUncommitDelay and what does it do?
cards.back: 300 seconds - how long unused heap must sit before uncommitting
cards.extra: Uncommitting returns memory to the OS. Re-committing is expensive, so too small a delay causes churn.
cards.example:
int delaySeconds = 300;
System.out.println("-XX:ZUncommitDelay=" + delaySeconds + "s");
System.out.println("unused heap must sit this long before uncommitting");

cards.front: Which ZGC option controls the assumed allocation spike factor, and what is its default?
cards.extra: A factor of 3.0 tells ZGC the allocation rate may triple at any moment, making it start collections earlier to stay ahead.
cards.example:
java -XX:+UseZGC -XX:ZAllocationSpikeTolerance=2.0 -version
# 2.0 is the default assumed allocation spike factor

cards.front: What is the recommended first step when adopting ZGC?
cards.back: Set -Xmx with headroom above the live set, and enable GC logging
cards.extra: ZGC needs little tuning; most gains come from headroom. Logging with -Xlog:gc is needed to compare against the previous collector.
cards.example:
java -XX:+UseZGC -Xmx16g -Xlog:gc -jar app.jar
# -Xmx leaves headroom above the live set; -Xlog:gc turns on GC logging

cards.front: Which ZGC option sets the number of concurrent GC threads?
cards.extra: ZGC has heuristics to pick it automatically, sized near a quarter of ParallelGC threads. Too many starves the app; too few lets garbage outpace collection.
cards.example:
String option = "-XX:ConcGCThreads"; // number of concurrent GC threads
System.out.println(option);

cards.front: Is ZGC a general upgrade over G1 that should improve every metric?
cards.back: No - it targets latency and huge live sets, and may regress other metrics
cards.extra: It was built for a niche, so throughput or footprint can get worse. It suits request-heavy web apps with large live sets and spare CPU.
cards.example:
java -XX:+UseZGC App   # targets latency and huge live sets
java -XX:+UseG1GC App  # switching to ZGC may regress other metrics

cards.front: Which GC is enabled by the JVM argument -XX:+UseZGC?
cards.extra: ZGC was experimental in JDK 11 and became production in JDK 15; pauses stay around one millisecond with heaps up to 16 TB.
cards.example:
String flag = "-XX:+UseZGC";
System.out.println(flag + " enables ZGC, the ultra-low-latency collector");

cards.front: What is jwebserver?
cards.back: A minimal JDK HTTP server serving one directory over HTTP/1.1
cards.extra: It serves static files only - no dynamic content, no other HTTP versions. Intended for prototyping, testing and debugging, not production.
cards.example:
String tool = "jwebserver";
System.out.println(tool + ": minimal JDK HTTP server");
System.out.println("serves one directory over HTTP/1.1");

cards.front: Which port does jwebserver listen on by default?
cards.extra: Change it with -p/--port. The served directory defaults to the current working directory (-d).
cards.example:
int defaultPort = 8000;
System.out.println("jwebserver default port: " + defaultPort);

cards.front: Which address does jwebserver bind to by default?
cards.extra: To expose all interfaces pass -b 0.0.0.0 (or -b ::). The default keeps the server invisible to the network.
cards.example:
jwebserver                # default bind: 127.0.0.1 or ::1 (loopback only)
jwebserver -b 0.0.0.0     # all interfaces instead

cards.front: Which HTTP methods does jwebserver serve?
cards.extra: Anything else gets 501 Not Implemented or 405 Not Allowed, so it cannot stand in for a write-capable API.
cards.example:
String[] methods = {"HEAD", "GET"}; // only idempotent methods
System.out.println(String.join(" and ", methods));

cards.front: What does jwebserver return for a directory with no index file?
cards.back: An HTML listing of file and subdirectory names
cards.extra: Hidden files and symbolic links are neither listed nor served, which keeps dotfiles from leaking over the wire.
cards.example:
jwebserver -d public      # public/ has no index file
curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/
# the response is an HTML listing of file and subdirectory names

cards.front: Which module contains jwebserver, and how else can you start it?
cards.extra: It wraps the com.sun.net.httpserver implementation, whose SimpleFileServer class lets you reuse the server programmatically.
cards.example:
jwebserver              # the tool lives in module jdk.httpserver
java -m jdk.httpserver  # the same tool started from its module

cards.front: What is the default value of jwebserver --output?
cards.extra: The three allowed values are none, info and verbose.
cards.example:
String output = "info";  // default for jwebserver --output
System.out.println(output);

cards.front: How does jwebserver decide the MIME type of .java files?
cards.back: A built-in table - it serves them as text/plain
cards.extra: MIME types are automatic, not configured. .html maps to text/html, and unknown extensions fall back to a generic binary type.
cards.example:
String source = "built-in table";
System.out.println("jwebserver MIME for .java: " + source + " -> text/plain");

cards.front: What does the jar tool let you do per entry to authenticate origin?
cards.extra: jar itself only packs and compresses. A signed JAR can then be verified entry by entry, and it stays a valid class-path entry.
cards.example:
String tool = "jarsigner";
System.out.println("sign individual JAR entries with " + tool + " to authenticate origin");

cards.front: What compression formats is the jar tool based on?
cards.extra: It is a general-purpose archiving tool whose syntax mirrors tar, with one mandatory main operation argument.
cards.example:
jar --create --file app.jar -C classes .   # the jar format is based on ZIP
# ZIP entry compression uses ZLIB

cards.front: Which jar flag creates, lists, and extracts an archive?
cards.extra: -u updates an existing archive; each is the short form of --create, --list, --extract, --update.
cards.example:
String create = "-c", list = "-t", extract = "-x";
System.out.println(create + " create, " + list + " list, " + extract + " extract");

cards.front: When does a JAR become a modular JAR?
cards.back: When a module-info.class is at the root of the archive
cards.extra: Only then do module-only options such as --module-version and --hash-modules apply.
cards.example:
import java.util.jar.JarFile;
class Ex { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
  JarFile jar = new JarFile("app.jar");
  System.out.println(jar.getJarEntry("module-info.class") != null); // modular JAR: at the root
} }

cards.front: Which jar option stores entries without ZIP compression?
cards.extra: Valid in create, update and generate-index modes. Uncompressed JARs load marginally faster but take far more space.
cards.example:
jar --create --file app.jar --no-compress -C classes .
jar -c -0 -f app.jar -C classes .   # -0 is the short form

cards.front: Which jar option embeds the application entry point for an executable JAR?
cards.extra: It writes the Main-Class manifest attribute. -m=FILE supplies a whole manifest instead, and -M omits it entirely.
cards.example:
String entry = "--main-class";   // jar -e=CLASSNAME: embed the application entry point
String[] args = {entry, "Main"}; // Main becomes the executable JAR's entry point

cards.front: Which jar option creates a multi-release JAR, and what does it do with the files?
cards.extra: VERSION must be an integer 9 or greater. At runtime the JDK picks the highest matching version folder, falling back to lower ones then the JAR root.
cards.example:
String version = "VERSION";  // jar --release VERSION: multi-release JAR
String path = "META-INF/versions/" + version + "/";
System.out.println(path);

cards.front: In an old release, what did jar originally package before JDK 9?
cards.extra: Since JDK 9 the same tool also builds modular JARs, which is the usual distribution unit for modules.
cards.example:
String[] packaged = {"applets", "applications"};
System.out.println(String.join(" and ", packaged));
// applets unsupported since JDK 11

cards.front: Which jar operation prints a module's descriptor or automatic module name?
cards.extra: It is the quick way to check the automatic module name derived from a non-modular JAR's filename before depending on it.
cards.example:
String describe = "--describe-module"; // also -d: prints a module descriptor or automatic module name
System.out.println(describe);
