cards.front: What are the two purposes of jarsigner?
cards.back: Sign JARs, and verify signatures and integrity of signed JARs
cards.extra: Signing is the default behaviour; -verify switches to checking. It works on any ZIP plus a META-INF/MANIFEST.MF.
cards.example:
String[] purposes = {"sign JARs", "verify signatures and integrity of signed JARs"};
for (String purpose : purposes) System.out.println(purpose);

cards.front: Which two files does signing add under META-INF?
cards.extra: The extension follows the key algorithm. Both files share a base name derived from the alias or from -sigfile.
cards.example:
jarsigner -keystore ks -signedjar signed.jar app.jar alias
unzip -l signed.jar | grep META-INF   # META-INF/ALIAS.SF and META-INF/ALIAS.RSA
# a .DSA or .EC block instead of .RSA for a DSA or EC signing key

cards.front: Without -sigfile, how are the signature file names derived?
cards.back: First 8 characters of the alias, uppercased
cards.extra: Invalid characters become underscores. Alias jane yields JANE.SF and JANE.RSA.
cards.example:
String alias = "MySigningAlias";
String baseName = alias.substring(0, 8).toUpperCase(); // first 8 chars, uppercased
System.out.println(baseName);

cards.front: What happens if no -signedjar is given when signing?
cards.back: The original JAR is overwritten by the signed version
cards.extra: Pass -signedjar file to keep the input untouched, which matters when the unsigned JAR is a build artifact you may want to re-sign.
cards.example:
jarsigner -keystore ks app.jar alias
# without -signedjar, the original JAR is overwritten by the signed version

cards.front: In a signed JAR, what does a signature file (.SF) record per source file?
cards.back: The file name, digest algorithm, and a digest of the manifest lines
cards.extra: Unlike the manifest, whose digest covers the file's bytes, the .SF digest covers that file's two manifest lines, chaining bytes to manifest to signature.
cards.example:
unzip -p signed.jar META-INF/ALIAS.SF
# Name: path/to/File.class
# SHA-256-Digest: digest of that file's two manifest lines

cards.front: Which file in a signed JAR carries the certificate chain used to verify it?
cards.extra: It holds the signed .SF plus the encoded certificate or chain, so verification needs no keystore - a keystore only lets you check who you trust.
cards.example:
String[] blockFiles = {".RSA", ".DSA", ".EC"};
System.out.println(String.join(" / ", blockFiles) + " carry the certificate chain");

cards.front: What is the default message digest algorithm for -digestalg?
cards.extra: Override with -digestalg only if an old consumer requires something else; defaults harden with each JDK release.
cards.example:
jarsigner -keystore ks app.jar alias                    # -digestalg defaults to SHA-256
jarsigner -keystore ks -digestalg SHA-256 app.jar alias  # stated explicitly

cards.front: A JAR was signed with an algorithm the JDK lists as disabled. How is it treated?
cards.extra: Legacy (not yet disabled) algorithms still verify but raise an informational warning. The lists live in the java.security file under $JAVA_HOME/conf/security.
cards.example:
boolean disabledAlgorithm = true;
boolean treatedAsSigned = !disabledAlgorithm; // disabled algorithm: treated as unsigned
System.out.println(treatedAsSigned);

cards.front: Where is the default keystore located for jarsigner and keytool?
cards.extra: Override with -keystore url. NONE means a null stream, for a keystore living on a hardware token.
cards.example:
String home = System.getProperty("user.home");
String defaultKeystore = home + "/.keystore";
System.out.println(defaultKeystore);

cards.front: What is the default keystore type in modern JDKs?
cards.extra: JKS remains a built-in Oracle implementation. The type comes from the keystore.type property or -storetype, and JKS and PKCS12 files are not interchangeable.
cards.example:
String defaultType = java.security.KeyStore.getDefaultType(); // PKCS12 in modern JDKs
System.out.println(defaultType);

cards.front: What exit code does a jarsigner failure produce?
cards.extra: Without -strict, severe warnings still exit 0. With -strict the exit code is the OR of warning codes, e.g. 12 means expired plus badKeyUsage.
cards.example:
int failureExitCode = 1;
System.out.println(failureExitCode);

cards.front: What does the -strict option change?
cards.back: Severe warnings become errors and affect the exit code
cards.extra: Messages then read 'jar signed, with signer errors'. Useful in CI, where an expired or disallowed certificate would otherwise pass silently.
cards.example:
jarsigner -strict -verify signed.jar
# severe warnings become errors and affect the exit code

cards.front: Which jarsigner option generates a signature time stamp?
cards.extra: The TSA is contacted with RFC 3161 TSP, and the returned token is stored in the signature block. Without a timestamp, verification fails after the certificate expires.
cards.example:
jarsigner -tsa url -keystore ks app.jar alias
jarsigner -tsacert alias -keystore ks app.jar alias
# generates a signature time stamp

cards.front: How do you sign a JAR with more than one person's signature?
cards.extra: Each run adds another .SF plus signature block pair. Verification then checks all of them, so a later unsigned change is caught regardless of who signed.
cards.example:
jarsigner -keystore ks app.jar alice
jarsigner -keystore ks app.jar bob
# run repeatedly, once per alias, for more than one signature

cards.front: In JAR verification, which two things must hold for success?
cards.back: Signatures are valid and no signed file has changed since signing
cards.extra: Files added after signing are tolerated - they are simply unsigned entries - and are reported as such by hasUnsignedEntry.
cards.example:
boolean signaturesValid = true;
boolean signedFilesUnchanged = true;
System.out.println(signaturesValid && signedFilesUnchanged); // both needed to verify

cards.front: What does keytool manage?
cards.back: A keystore: keys, X.509 certificate chains, and trusted certificates
cards.extra: It also stores secret keys and passphrases for symmetric crypto, which is why commands like -genseckey and -importpass exist.
cards.example:
keytool -list -keystore demo.p12
# a keystore holds keys, X.509 certificate chains and trusted certificates

cards.front: What kind of certificate does keytool -genkeypair produce?
cards.back: A self-signed X.509 v3 certificate, a one-element chain
cards.extra: keytool generates v3 certificates but can import v1, v2 and v3. The self-signed chain is replaced later by the CA's reply via -importcert.
cards.example:
keytool -genkeypair -alias demo -keyalg RSA -keystore demo.p12
keytool -list -v -alias demo -keystore demo.p12   # self-signed X.509 v3, a one-element chain

cards.front: Which keytool command generates a key pair?
cards.extra: It wraps the public key in a self-signed X.509 v3 certificate stored as a one-element chain under the alias.
cards.example:
keytool -genkeypair -alias a -keystore ks
# generates a key pair

cards.front: Which keytool command creates a CSR?
cards.back: -certreq - a PKCS #10 request signed with the alias's private key
cards.extra: The CA authenticates the requester (usually offline) and returns a certificate or chain, which you install with -importcert.
cards.example:
String command = "-certreq";             // keytool: PKCS #10 certificate request
String signedBy = "alias's private key"; // signed with that key
System.out.println(command + " - " + signedBy);

cards.front: Which keytool command installs the CA's reply over the self-signed certificate?
cards.extra: If the alias points to a key entry it is treated as a certificate reply; if it does not, the alias becomes a trusted-certificate entry instead.
cards.example:
keytool -importcert -alias a -keystore ks -file ca-reply.cer
# installs the CA reply over the self-signed certificate

cards.front: What is the keytool default validity, in days?
cards.extra: Defaults vary by algorithm: 256 for EC, 255 for EdDSA (Ed25519), 56 for DES and 168 for DESede secret keys; RSA is the common case.
cards.example:
int defaultValidityDays = 90;
System.out.println("keytool default validity: " + defaultValidityDays + " days");

cards.front: What is keytool's default -keysize for an RSA key pair?
cards.extra: Defaults differ by algorithm: 256 for EC, 255 for EdDSA (Ed25519), 56 for DES and 168 for DESede secret keys.
cards.example:
int defaultKeySize = 2048;  // keytool default -keysize for an RSA key pair
System.out.println(defaultKeySize + " bits");

cards.front: Which keytool option prints the default SHA-256 fingerprint of a certificate?
cards.extra: Adding -v prints the human-readable detail: owner, issuer, serial number and extensions. -rfc prints PEM instead.
cards.example:
keytool -list -keystore ks    # without -v: default SHA-256 fingerprint
keytool -list -v -keystore ks # verbose form, for comparison

cards.front: Can you pass both -v and -rfc to keytool -list?
cards.extra: They are different output modes: verbose is human-readable detail, rfc is base64 PEM, so they cannot be combined.
cards.example:
keytool -list -v -keystore ks       # verbose output
keytool -list -rfc -keystore ks     # RFC-style output
keytool -list -v -rfc -keystore ks  # error: -v and -rfc cannot be combined

cards.front: Which keytool command inspects a certificate file, an SSL server, or a signed JAR?
cards.extra: If no port is given, 443 is assumed. -file and -sslserver cannot be combined.
cards.example:
keytool -printcert -file cert.cer        # inspect a certificate file
keytool -printcert -sslserver host:443   # inspect an SSL server
keytool -printcert -jarfile app.jar      # inspect a signed JAR

cards.front: Where does keytool look for the system trust store (the cacerts file)?
cards.extra: It is a system-wide keystore of root CA certificates. -cacerts is shorthand for -keystore .../cacerts -storetype jks.
cards.example:
String javaHome = "$JAVA_HOME";
String cacerts = javaHome + "/lib/security/cacerts";
System.out.println(cacerts);

cards.front: What is the initial password of the JDK's cacerts file?
cards.extra: It is the normal way to convert between keystore types, for example JKS to PKCS12, or to move entries onto a PKCS #11 hardware token.
cards.example:
String initialPassword = "changeit";
System.out.println(initialPassword);

cards.front: Which command imports all entries from one keystore into another?
cards.extra: It is the normal way to convert, for example, a JKS store to PKCS12, or to move entries onto a PKCS #11 hardware token.
cards.example:
keytool -importkeystore -srckeystore src.p12 -destkeystore dst.p12
# imports all entries from one keystore into another

cards.front: What does keytool -exportcert output by default, and what does -rfc change?
cards.back: Binary DER by default; -rfc gives Base64 PEM
cards.extra: PEM output is bounded by -----BEGIN / -----END lines, which is what most mailers and web servers accept.
cards.example:
String cmd = "-exportcert";
String rfc = "-rfc";
System.out.println(cmd + ": binary DER by default; " + rfc + ": Base64 PEM");

cards.front: What does keytool -genkeypair use as the issuer and subject of the generated certificate?
cards.back: The value of -dname, prompting for it if omitted
cards.extra: Order matters in a DN - cn, ou, o, l, st, c, like cn=myname, ou=mygroup, o=mycompany, c=mycountry.
cards.example:
keytool -genkeypair -alias a -dname "CN=Example" -keystore ks
# issuer and subject of the certificate: the -dname value
keytool -genkeypair -alias a -keystore ks
# prompts for -dname when omitted

cards.front: What is the minimum length of a keytool password?
cards.extra: The tools scan installed providers for one implementing that type. JKS and PKCS12 are not binary compatible and need conversion via -importkeystore.
cards.example:
int minimum = 6;                    // keytool passwords: at least six characters
boolean accepted = "abcdef".length() >= minimum;
System.out.println(accepted);

cards.front: Without -storetype, how do keytool and jarsigner choose the implementation?
cards.extra: The tools then scan installed providers for one implementing that type. JKS and PKCS12 stores are not binary compatible and need conversion.
cards.example:
String setting = "keystore.type in java.security";
String fallback = "pkcs12";
System.out.println(setting + "; default " + fallback + " without -storetype");

cards.front: Which keytool option lets you add an X.509 extension, and can it repeat?
cards.extra: That is why it may be given many times, e.g. -ext SAN=dns:example.com,ip:10.0.0.1 plus -ext KU=keyEncipherment.
cards.example:
keytool -genkeypair -alias a -keystore ks -ext SAN=dns:example.com -ext KU=keyEncipherment
# -ext is the only multi-valued option: repeat it for each extension

cards.front: Which keytool command lists TLS protocols and cipher suites?
cards.extra: It reports the enabled TLS configuration rather than any keystore content, which makes it a handy way to check what a JDK will negotiate.
cards.example:
keytool -showinfo -tls
# lists TLS protocols and cipher suites

cards.front: Which command prints the contents of a PKCS #10 certificate request?
cards.extra: That flexibility is deliberate, for self-signed test certificates, but such certificates may be rejected by the JDK and by other applications.
cards.example:
keytool -printcertreq -file request.csr
# prints the contents of the PKCS #10 certificate request

cards.front: Why does keytool warn that it can generate non-conforming certificates?
cards.back: It does not enforce all X.509 profile rules
cards.extra: That flexibility is deliberate, for self-signed test certificates, but such certificates may be rejected by the JDK or other apps.
cards.example:
boolean enforcesAllProfileRules = false;
System.out.println("warning: non-conforming certificates");
// keytool does not enforce all X.509 profile rules

cards.front: How many keytool commands can appear in one invocation?
cards.extra: Options for that command may come in any order; repeating a single-valued option silently keeps the last value given.
cards.example:
int commandsPerInvocation = 1;  // keytool: exactly one command
System.out.println(commandsPerInvocation);

cards.front: What does kinit obtain?
cards.extra: The user must already be registered as a principal with the KDC. The tool is compatible with MIT and SEAM-style kinit.
cards.example:
kinit alice@EXAMPLE.COM   # obtains a ticket-granting ticket
klist                     # the TGT is cached locally

cards.front: Which kinit flag issues a forwardable ticket, and which a proxiable one?
cards.extra: These grant the ticket extra delegation powers; both can be combined, e.g. when a service must act on behalf of the user.
cards.example:
kinit -f alice@EXAMPLE.COM   # -f issues a forwardable ticket
kinit -p alice@EXAMPLE.COM   # -p issues a proxiable ticket

cards.front: Which kinit flag renews an existing renewable ticket?
cards.extra: A ticket must be renewed before it expires. Repeated renewals are possible only until the renewable lifetime set by -r runs out.
cards.example:
kinit -R
# renews an existing renewable ticket

cards.front: Which kinit option sets how long a ticket can be renewed for?
cards.extra: Distinct from -l lifetime, which sets how long one ticket is valid. Lifetimes accept h:m:s, NdNhNmNs, or a bare number.
cards.example:
String option = "-r";        // kinit sets the renewable lifetime
String value = "renewable_time";
System.out.println(option + " " + value);

cards.front: Why must you never pass a Kerberos password to kinit -password in a script?
cards.back: It is for testing only; a real password would be compromised
cards.extra: The fallback path is built from the user.home system property, so a daemon started with an unexpected home directory looks in the wrong place.
cards.example:
# -password is for testing only: a real password in a script is compromised
kinit -password *** alice@EXAMPLE.COM

cards.front: Where does kinit get the keytab name when -t is not given?
cards.extra: The fallback path is built from the user.home system property, so a daemon started with an odd home directory looks in the wrong place.
cards.example:
String fromConfig = null; // no -t: kinit reads the Kerberos config
String fallback = System.getProperty("user.home") + "\\krb5.keytab";
String keytab = fromConfig != null ? fromConfig : fallback;

cards.front: What does klist display?
cards.back: Entries in the local credentials cache and keytab
cards.extra: It is read-only: it never modifies the Kerberos database, which makes it the safe default diagnosis step.
cards.example:
klist
# displays entries in the local credentials cache and keytab

cards.front: Which klist flags list the credential cache and the keytab, respectively?
cards.back: -c for the cache, -k for the keytab
cards.extra: Add -e to show the encryption type, -f for credential flags and -a for addresses in cache listings.
cards.example:
String cacheFlag = "-c";   // credential cache
String keytabFlag = "-k";  // keytab
System.out.println(cacheFlag + " cache, " + keytabFlag + " keytab");

cards.front: After changing a keytab with ktab, how can you confirm the change?
cards.extra: Both are local inspection only. Nothing in the KDC changes, so the KDC side has to be updated separately.
cards.example:
String[] verify = {"klist -k", "ktab -l"}; // list the keytab after a ktab change
for (String command : verify) System.out.println(command);

cards.front: What is a Kerberos keytab?
cards.back: A host's copy of its own principals and keys - analogous to a password
cards.extra: A server that must authenticate itself to the KDC (e.g. a service principal) needs a keytab containing its own principal and key.
cards.example:
class Keytab {
    String[] principals;  // the host's own principals
    String[] keys;        // and their keys, like a password for the host
}

cards.front: How must a keytab file be stored to be safe?
cards.back: On local disk, readable only by root, never sent over a network in clear
cards.extra: Anyone who reads a keytab can impersonate the service without knowing its password, so file permissions are the whole security boundary.
cards.example:
chmod 600 /etc/security/keytabs/svc.keytab   # local disk, readable only by root
# never send the keytab over a network in clear text

cards.front: Do ktab changes affect the Kerberos database?
cards.back: No - none of its operations touch the KDC
cards.extra: If you change keys in the keytab you must make the matching change in the Kerberos database, and vice versa, or the service cannot authenticate.
cards.example:
boolean touchesKdc = false; // no ktab operation touches the Kerberos database
System.out.println(touchesKdc);

cards.front: Which ktab option lists entries with timestamps, and which with encryption types?
cards.extra: Both can be combined: ktab -l -e -t shows the keytab name, entries, types and timestamps.
cards.example:
ktab -l -t
# lists entries with timestamps
ktab -l -e
# lists entries with encryption types

cards.front: What does ktab -d principal old delete?
cards.back: All keys except those with the highest kvno
cards.extra: The default action is all. old is the safe rotation choice - it retires superseded keys while keeping the current one working.
cards.example:
ktab -l alice@EXAMPLE.COM       # list keys before the change
ktab -d alice@EXAMPLE.COM old   # deletes all keys except the highest kvno

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::13 JVM and Tooling::03 Core JDK Tools

cards.front: How does the java launcher start an application in three steps?
cards.back: Start the JRE, load the specified class, call its main()
cards.extra: main must be public static void taking a String[]. Overloads taking String... also work, since varargs compile down to an array parameter.
cards.example:
class App {
    public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("JRE started; App loaded; main() called"); }
}

cards.front: With java -jar app.jar, how is the entry class determined?
cards.extra: When -jar is used the JAR is the entire class path and any -cp setting is ignored - a classic 'class not found' trap.
cards.example:
jar --create --file app.jar --main-class com.example.App -C classes .
java -jar app.jar
# the entry class comes from the Main-Class header in META-INF/MANIFEST.MF

cards.front: What selects source-file mode in the java launcher?
cards.back: An existing .java file as first non-option arg, or --source N
cards.extra: The file is compiled in memory and the first top-level class found is executed. No .class file is written.
cards.example:
java Hello.java                  # existing .java first non-option arg selects source-file mode
java --source 21 Hello.java      # --source N selects it too

cards.front: In source-file mode, is annotation processing run?
cards.extra: Only the file named on the command line is compiled, the source path is effectively empty, so Lombok-style processors and -Werror tricks do not run.
cards.example:
java --source 21 Tool.java
# in source-file mode annotation processing is disabled, as if -proc:none

cards.front: Which environment variable prepends options to every java launch?
cards.extra: Its content is parsed as if it appeared before the command line, and the launcher prints a reminder to stderr when it is set.
cards.example:
JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS="-Xmx512m" java -version
# the variable prepends its options to every java launch

cards.front: Can JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS contain -jar or -h?
cards.back: No - the launcher aborts with an error
cards.extra: Main-class selectors and exit-without-running options are disallowed to stop an environment variable from hijacking which application is launched.
cards.example:
JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS="-jar" java -version
# the launcher aborts with an error: -jar and -h are not allowed there

cards.front: Which prefix marks Extra options for HotSpot, and which prefix marks Advanced options?
cards.extra: Standard options are guaranteed on every JVM. Both -X and -XX are HotSpot-specific, subject to change, and not portable.
cards.example:
java -Xmx512m -XX:+UseZGC -version
# -X marks Extra options; -XX marks Advanced HotSpot options

cards.front: How do you enable and disable a boolean -XX option?
cards.extra: Boolean options take no value. For valued options the syntax varies: space, : or = may all be the separator.
cards.example:
java -XX:+UseZGC -version   # + enables a boolean -XX option
java -XX:-UseZGC -version   # - disables it

cards.front: You pass -XX:MaxHeapFreeRatio=25 meaning 25%. Is that right?
cards.back: Yes — the value is a percentage from 0 to 100, so 25 means 25%; 0.25 is rejected as an improperly specified VM option
cards.extra: The JVM would read 25 literally and reject it as out of range, which the flag validator reports at startup.
cards.example:
java -XX:MinHeapFreeRatio=10 -XX:MaxHeapFreeRatio=25 -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version
# reports MaxHeapFreeRatio = 25: 25 percent, not 0.25
# java -XX:MaxHeapFreeRatio=0.25 -> improperly specified VM option

cards.front: Are assertions enabled by default by the java launcher?
cards.back: No - disabled in all packages and classes
cards.extra: Enable globally with -ea or per package/class with -ea:com.foo.... Ordering matters: later switches override earlier ones.
cards.example:
boolean enabledByLauncher = false;   // assertions are disabled in all packages and classes by default
assert false : "not evaluated by default";
System.out.println(enabledByLauncher);

cards.front: Which switch enables or disables assertions?
cards.extra: Both apply to all class loaders, but with no argument they skip system classes; -esa and -dsa target system classes.
cards.example:
java -ea App   # enables assertions
java -da App   # disables assertions

cards.front: Which launcher option loads a native agent library by name?
cards.extra: -agentpath does the same with an absolute path. -javaagent:jarpath is the pure-Java equivalent.
cards.example:
java -agentlib:jdwp=transport=dt_socket,server=y -jar app.jar
# -agentlib:libname[=options] loads a native agent library by name

cards.front: Is a @argfile useful for getting around command-line length limits?
cards.back: Yes - the launcher expands its contents before argument processing
cards.extra: Files are expanded after shell expansion. The argument file may even hold the main class and all options, so the command shrinks to java @file.
cards.example:
java @long-args.txt -jar app.jar
# the launcher expands the file before argument processing, avoiding command-line length limits

cards.front: Which launcher option prints ergonomically chosen JVM flags?
cards.extra: You then see the heap size and the collector the JVM actually picked, rather than guessing what ergonomics resolved the defaults to.
cards.example:
java -XX:+PrintCommandLineFlags -version
# prints the ergonomically chosen JVM flags

cards.front: Which option sets the thread stack size, and what is the Linux/x64 default?
cards.extra: Raise it for deep recursion; shrink it to allow many more threads, since each platform thread reserves this from virtual memory.
cards.example:
java -Xss1024k -version
# -Xss (or -XX:ThreadStackSize=1024) sets the thread stack size; Linux/x64 default 1024 KB

cards.front: Which fix eliminates a StackOverflowError from deep recursion?
cards.back: Raise -Xss, or restructure the algorithm to be iterative — virtual threads still have stacks that can overflow
cards.extra: Raising the stack defers the problem. A deeper point: virtual threads get their own growable stack, so stack size stops being the hard limit.
cards.example:
java -Xss2m MyApp   # raise -Xss to give deep recursion more stack
# or restructure to iterative / use virtual threads

cards.front: Which heap option sets the initial and minimum heap size?
cards.extra: -Xmx (same as -XX:MaxHeapSize) sets the maximum. For server deployments both are often set equal to avoid resizing.
cards.example:
java -Xms256m -cp . App
# initial and minimum heap size is 256 MB

cards.front: Which flag reveals whether compressed oops are active, given heap below 32 GB?
cards.extra: -XX:-UseCompressedOops disables them. They convert references to 32-bit offsets and are on by default under a 32 GB heap.
cards.example:
java -XX:+PrintCommandLineFlags -version
java -XshowSettings:vm -version
# with a heap under ~32 GB these show whether compressed oops are active

cards.front: What is the default value of -XX:ObjectAlignmentInBytes?
cards.extra: It must be a power of 2 between 8 and 256. Raising it stretches the addressable range of compressed oops beyond the usual 32 GB heap limit.
cards.example:
java -XX:ObjectAlignmentInBytes=8 -version
# the default value of -XX:ObjectAlignmentInBytes is 8 bytes

cards.front: Which option writes a heap dump on the first OutOfMemoryError?
cards.extra: The dump goes to the working directory; set the destination with -XX:HeapDumpPath. It is disabled by default.
cards.example:
java -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError MyApp
# writes a heap dump on the first OutOfMemoryError

cards.front: What does -XX:+DisableExplicitGC do to System.gc() calls?
cards.back: Ignores them; the JVM still collects when it decides to
cards.extra: Useful because explicit GCs are usually a full stop-the-world collection, often triggered by libraries rather than application logic.
cards.example:
System.gc();   // a request only
System.out.println("with -XX:+DisableExplicitGC the JVM ignores it and collects when it decides");

cards.front: Where does the JVM write the crash log after an irrecoverable error?
cards.extra: Override the path with -XX:ErrorFile. -XX:+ExtensiveErrorReports adds more detail, and -XX:OnError runs a command such as gcore.
cards.example:
java MyApp
# after an irrecoverable error the JVM writes hs_err_pid<pid>.log in the working directory

cards.front: Which option links a command to run when an OOM error occurs?
cards.extra: Semicolon-separated commands, %p expands to the PID. Common uses are dumping a core or bouncing the container.
cards.example:
java -XX:OnOutOfMemoryError="kill -9 %p" -jar app.jar
# %p is the JVM process id; the command runs when an OOM occurs

cards.front: What is the default for -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis per the launcher reference?
cards.back: No maximum pause value by default
cards.extra: G1 docs describe it as a soft goal. On some collectors the default is 200 ms; either way the JVM makes a best effort, not a guarantee.
cards.example:
java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep MaxGCPauseMillis
# per the launcher reference: no maximum pause value by default

cards.front: Which option enables the attach mechanism by default, and how do you turn it off?
cards.extra: Turning it off blocks tools like jcmd, jstack, jmap and jinfo from attaching, which is done in locked-down or abandoned-wasro deployments.
cards.example:
jcmd $PID Thread.print   # attach works by default
java -XX:+DisableAttachMechanism -jar app.jar   # turns the attach mechanism off

cards.front: You want jcmd/jstack to stop working on a production JVM. Which flag?
cards.extra: Note the counter-intuitive polarity: the flag is phrased as a positive, but it disables the feature, which is off by default as a flag.
cards.example:
java -XX:+DisableAttachMechanism -jar app.jar
# jcmd and jstack can no longer attach to this JVM

cards.front: What format does the unified logging option -Xlog use?
cards.extra: Example: -Xlog:gc=debug:file=gc.log:none. The deprecated -Xloggc:file is the same as -Xlog:gc:file.
cards.example:
java -Xlog:gc=info:stdout:time,uptime -version
# tag=level : output : decorators

cards.front: Which decorators does -Xlog apply when none are specified?
cards.extra: Change them at runtime; the special none decorator turns all decorations off, as in -Xlog:gc=debug:none.
cards.example:
java -Xlog:gc -version
# when no decorators are specified, -Xlog applies uptime, level and tags

cards.front: Which -Xlog tag combination does gc+heap select?
cards.back: Messages with both tags; gc,heap is a union, gc* a prefix
cards.extra: Mixing them up is the usual reason a log appears empty. -Xlog:disable first resets everything to off before adding selections.
cards.example:
java -Xlog:gc+heap=info -version   # messages with both tags
java -Xlog:gc,heap=info -version   # union: either tag
java -Xlog:gc*=info -version       # prefix: tags starting with gc

cards.front: What do @argfile and --disable-@files do together?
cards.extra: The stop option can appear anywhere, including inside an argument file, which is how a launcher script controls which nested files are trusted.
cards.example:
printf '%s\n' -Xmx512m -jar app.jar > args.txt
java @args.txt                    # launcher expands the file's arguments
java --disable-@files @args.txt   # expansion disabled

cards.front: Which option prints the range of every JVM flag?
cards.extra: The JVM validates all flag values - set ergonomically, on the command line, or via jcmd - and terminates with an error if a value is out of range.
cards.example:
java -XX:+PrintFlagsRanges -version
# prints the range of every JVM flag

cards.front: Why do large (huge) pages help the JVM?
cards.back: They reduce TLB misses by covering more memory per page-table entry
cards.extra: The TLB is a small cache of virtual-to-physical translations, and misses cost several memory accesses. Linux and Windows support large pages.
cards.example:
int smallPages = 1024;   // 4 MB as 4 KB pages
int hugePages = 1;       // 4 MB as one large page
System.out.println(smallPages + " vs " + hugePages + " page-table entries");   // fewer entries -> fewer TLB misses

cards.front: Which options put the object heap on large pages?
cards.back: -XX:+UseLargePages — +UseHugeTLBFS is its equivalent, and +UseSHM is the Linux shared-memory alternative
cards.extra: They require root-level OS setup (vm.nr_hugepages), and pages are pre-allocated up front, so the heap cannot grow dynamically.
cards.example:
java -XX:+UseLargePages -XX:+UseHugeTLBFS -cp . App
java -XX:+UseLargePages -XX:+UseSHM -cp . App
# Linux: huge pages preallocated, or large pages via shared memory

cards.front: Which set of steps produce a dynamic CDS archive?
cards.extra: The archive captures classes loaded during a single trial run, so the trial run step AppCDS needs is eliminated. It still needs a base archive.
cards.example:
java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=x.jsa -jar app.jar
java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=x.jsa -jar app.jar

cards.front: Which option turns CDS off entirely?
cards.extra: -Xshare:auto uses it when possible, -Xshare:on fails if it cannot. Class data sharing cuts startup time and footprint.
cards.example:
java -Xshare:off -cp . App
# CDS is off for this launch

cards.front: Which option unlocks the diagnostic JVM options?
cards.extra: Options like -XX:+LogCompilation require it. Diagnostic flags are developer-only and not guaranteed across releases.
cards.example:
java -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+LogCompilation -cp . App
# LogCompilation is diagnostic; the first flag unlocks such options

batches.deck: 00 Java Roadmap::12 Documentation::02 Certifications and Validation

cards.front: Which exam is the current newest Java certification exam?
cards.extra: 50 questions in 120 minutes, passing score 68%. The prior ones are 1Z0-830 (Java 21) and 1Z0-829 (Java 17), both 50 questions and 68%.
cards.example:
Newest active exam: 1Z0-831 Java SE 25 Developer Professional
1Z0-830 is the Java SE 21 exam

cards.front: How many questions and what pass mark does the 1Z0-831 (Java SE 25) exam have?
cards.extra: The 1Z0-830 (Java 21) and 1Z0-829 (Java 17) exams use the same 50 questions and 68% bar, so a mock result maps directly onto them.
cards.example:
1Z0-831 Java SE 25 Developer Professional
50 questions in 120 minutes, pass mark 68%

cards.front: How many parts did the Java 8 developer certification have?
cards.extra: 808 is 56 questions at 65%, 809 is 68 questions at 65%. Splitting the exam is unique to Java 8 - the Java 11 exam started split but was merged.
cards.example:
Java SE 8 developer certification: 1Z0-808 + 1Z0-809
one certification for each half

cards.front: Should you wait for the next LTS exam before starting to study?
cards.back: No - take whichever exam is available when you start
cards.extra: Objectives and study materials lag an LTS release by months, and passing without materials is much harder; newer syntax is a small gain.
cards.example:
Take the exam available when you start studying
not the next LTS exam
study materials for a future exam take months to appear

cards.front: You hold Java 21 study materials. Which exam should you target?
cards.extra: Materials must match the exam version, because objectives change between releases. Studying Java 21 books for the Java 25 exam leaves gaps.
cards.example:
Java 21 study materials -> target 1Z0-830
the Java SE 21 Developer Professional exam

cards.front: What is the format of the Java 11 exam 1Z0-819?
cards.back: One consolidated exam, replacing the earlier 815/816 split
cards.extra: Java 8 launched its exam in two parts and Java 11 began that way too, then merged into the single 1Z0-819, with 50 questions and a 68% pass mark.
cards.example:
1Z0-819 Java SE 11 Developer
one consolidated exam, replacing the earlier 1Z0-815 + 1Z0-816 split

cards.front: Which certification is the Oracle Academy Java Foundations exam?
cards.extra: It is far less common than the developer exams and is positioned as an easier first certification before the 829, 830 or 831.
cards.example:
1Z0-811 Java Foundations (Oracle Academy)
60 questions, pass mark 65%, based on Java 8

cards.front: What practice technique is recommended before attempting the real exam?
cards.extra: Mocks expose the precise API recall the exam rewards and produce a score comparable to the real 68% pass bar. Writing code matters too.
cards.example:
Enthuware mock exams: 20 mock exams
recommended practice after studying, before the real exam
